key_insight: Channel geometry alone can strongly tune capillary-driven transport and analyte confinement in paper-based microdevices, with circular channels moving fastest and diverging-converging designs retaining analytes most effectively.
engineering_relevance: The results provide design guidance for low-cost diagnostic paper devices by showing how geometric shaping can control flow speed, residence time, and preconcentration without active pumping.
method: Compared five paper-channel geometries: converging-diverging, diverging-converging, wide-to-narrow, circular, and rectangular.
Measured capillary flow using fluorescent model analytes pyrene and benz[α]anthracene under UV quantification.
Validated geometry-adapted Lucas--Washburn predictions with calibrated CFD and mesh-independence checks.
evidence_signal: Experimental transport times spanned 23.1 s to 65.0 s, with pyrene mean velocities from 0.571 mm/s in circular channels to 0.284 mm/s in diverging-converging channels, and CFD matched the observed velocity distributions semi-quantitatively.
watch_item: Because analyte retention was also influenced by cyclodextrin-functionalized chitosan coatings, geometric effects should be interpreted alongside surface-chemistry interactions in real assay conditions.
paper_title: Geometry-Driven Passive Fluid Transport in Paper-Based Microdevices
